summary: Adapts the Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers ideas to reduce delay and packet loss when a Mobile IPv4 device changes networks. It targets movement detection, IP address configuration, and location update latency. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: When a phone moves from one wifi to another, this tries to make the switch quicker so less gets lost.

questions: reduce packet loss during mobile ip handoff
how to reduce mobile ipv4 handover delay
subtitle: Reducing delay and packet loss when Mobile IPv4 devices switch between networks.

tldr.problem: When a mobile IPv4 device moves from one network to another (from one access point to another), three sources of delay occur: detection of the movement, configuration of a new IP address, and registration of the new location with the home agent. These delays cause packet loss and interruption of real-time applications like voice calls.
tldr.mechanism: The protocol allows a mobile node to discover the next network and address before disconnecting from the current one, so it can start using the new address immediately upon attachment. Access routers exchange information to establish a tunnel for the old address, allowing packets sent to the old location to reach the node on the new network while registration happens asynchronously.
tldr.outcome: Handover latency is significantly reduced by decoupling address configuration and IP-layer registration from the time-critical switching period, and by pre-establishing routing support at access routers.

today: RFC 4988 is an Experimental protocol. It provides the specification for fast handovers in Mobile IPv4. Like Mobile IPv4 itself, it remains in use for mobile devices that need to maintain connectivity across network transitions, though it is not a standard. Newer protocols such as Mobile IPv6 and LISP are also used for mobility.

sections.title: The Handover Problem
sections.content:
Mobile IPv4 (RFC 3344) allows mobile hosts to maintain network connectivity while moving between networks. However, when a mobile node changes its network attachment point—moving from one access point to another, or from one wireless network to another—significant delays and packet loss occur. The protocol is adapted from Mobile IPv6 Fast Handovers (RFC 4068) to address these delays in IPv4 networks.

When a mobile node moves to a new network, it becomes known as a handover. The mobile node must change its Care-of Address (CoA): either obtaining a new address via DHCP (if using co-located mode) or using the new access router's address (if using foreign agent mode). After obtaining a new CoA, the mobile node must notify its home agent of the change. All of these steps create latency. Real-time applications like Voice over IP are particularly sensitive to this handover delay.
sections.eli5: When you move your phone from one wifi to another, your phone has to figure out its new address, tell your phone's home company, and get packets flowing again. That takes time and some calls drop.

sections.title: What Causes Handover Delays
sections.content:
Three IP-layer delays affect handover performance. Movement detection latency is the time to reliably detect that the node has moved to a new subnet. This depends on how often the access router sends link-layer advertisements and the timeout for detecting loss of connectivity. IP address configuration latency depends on whether the node is using DHCP (which can be slow) or is assigned a pre-configured address. Mobile IP registration latency is the round-trip delay to send a binding update to the home agent and receive acknowledgment, which happens over the internet.

Beyond IP operations, link-layer procedures also affect handover. In wireless networks such as IEEE 802.11, the mobile node must scan for access points, select one, and perform association, which may include authentication steps. Optimizations at the link layer (such as those in IEEE 802.11r and IEEE 802.21) can reduce this overhead. The protocol specified in this RFC focuses on reducing IP-layer delays, assuming link-layer optimizations are handled separately.
sections.eli5: Three things slow down the switch: figuring out you moved, getting a new address, and telling your home agent. Each can take milliseconds to seconds, and together they add up.

sections.title: The Fast Handover Protocol Design
sections.content:
The protocol avoids handover delay by decoupling operations. First, before a handover, the mobile node sends a Router Solicitation for Proxy Advertisement (RtSolPr) to the current access router, requesting information about neighboring networks. The access router responds with a Proxy Router Advertisement (PrRtAdv) listing neighboring access points and routers, including their addresses and network prefixes. The mobile node can use this information to determine which network it is moving to even before it loses connection to the current one.

Second, the mobile node sends a Fast Binding Update (FBU) to the current access router (the Previous Access Router, or PAR), indicating that it will move to a new network and listing the new access router's (NAR's) address. The PAR coordinates with the NAR by sending Handover Initiate (HI) and Handover Acknowledge (HAck) messages to establish a tunnel. Once this is set up, packets arriving at the PAR destined for the mobile node are tunneled to the NAR, where they are delivered to the newly arrived mobile node. This allows the mobile node to receive packets immediately, even though the formal binding update to the home agent is still in progress.
sections.eli5: Before jumping, your phone gets a map of nearby networks. When it decides to move, it tells the current network 'I'm going there' and asks the new network to get ready. A tunnel is set up so packets keep flowing while formal registration happens later.

sections.title: Predictive and Reactive Handover
sections.content:
The protocol supports two modes of operation. In predictive mode, the mobile node sends the FBU while still connected to the PAR, allowing the access routers to establish the tunnel before the actual network switch occurs. The mobile node specifies the NAR's address (learned from the PrRtAdv) as the new CoA in the FBU. When the node detects the link to the PAR is lost, it connects to the NAR and begins receiving packets immediately through the established tunnel.

In reactive mode, the mobile node does not send the FBU until after connecting to the new network. It sends the FBU directly to the NAR, which then forwards it to the PAR. This allows recovery if predictive mode is not possible, though it adds some delay since the tunnel is established after attachment rather than before.

The PAR and NAR use the HI and HAck messages to establish a bidirectional tunnel that supports packet forwarding for the mobile node's previous CoA. The tunnel is established in response to receiving the FBU. The access routers can also optionally provide a new CoA for the mobile node to use, supplied by the NAR in the HAck and forwarded to the node in the FBU acknowledgment.
sections.eli5: Two ways: tell the old network before you jump (predictive), so it is ready, or tell it right after you land (reactive). Either way, the handoff is faster because the routers coordinated instead of waiting for you to tell the home agent far away.

sections.title: Protocol Messages
sections.content:
Five main message types are used. The RtSolPr message is sent by the mobile node to request information about neighboring networks, and the PrRtAdv response contains tuples of access point identifiers, access router addresses, and prefix information. Both use ICMP format.

The FBU (Fast Binding Update) is based on the Mobile IPv4 registration request format and sent to port 434. It contains the mobile node's home address (or current CoA), the PAR's address, and the NAR's address as the new CoA. The FBAck (Fast Binding Acknowledgment) is the reply, confirming that the binding was accepted and optionally providing a new CoA. Both include authentication extensions to prevent spoofing.

The HI (Handover Initiate) and HAck (Handover Acknowledge) messages are exchanged between the PAR and NAR to establish the tunnel. They also use ICMP format. The HI contains the link-layer address of the mobile node, its previous CoA, and optionally its desired new CoA. The HAck confirms acceptance and may provide a new CoA if the 'S' flag is set in the HI.
sections.eli5: Messages are sent: 'what networks are nearby?' → 'here is a map'. Then 'I am moving there' → 'got it, start forwarding'. And between routers: 'there is a client coming' → 'ready to receive'.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The protocol introduces security considerations beyond those of standard Mobile IPv4. The FBU and FBAck messages require authentication to prevent unauthorized binding updates. The RFC specifies that authentication is performed using a shared key between the mobile node and the PAR, distributed by other means (such as RFC 3957). This prevents an attacker from hijacking the mobile node's traffic by sending false binding updates.

The HI and HAck messages between routers must be protected to ensure that only authorized routers can establish tunnels. The access routers must verify each other's identity and establish secure tunneling to prevent traffic interception or redirection. The details of router-to-router security and key distribution are not fully specified in this RFC and are assumed to be handled by the deployment environment.
sections.eli5: Messages are signed so only the right phone can change its binding, and only real routers can set up tunnels. This prevents someone else from stealing the connection.
